I shall not move my husband named Rukmangada from truth, goddess. Truth alone is declared the giver of the goal to men.
naradapuran:156:67	A man fallen from truth the wise regard as lower than a dog-cooker.
Having said so, she, golden-bright, with red fingers and fair brows, seized with both hands the feet of her husband (spoken of as) Mohini's... daughter of the lotus-born.
Having so spoken, the king then came near his beloved Sandhyavali and said to Mohini:
I said before, 'You must eat on Hari's day.' Rule the earth at will for many years, O king.
I would not have your son killed; my aim is accomplished by your eating. For me, lord of the earth, the work is not your son's death.
If the son is dear to you, O king, eat on Hari's day. What is the use of these laments, which are outside dharma, O protector of the earth?
Guard truth with effort and do my word." To her thus speaking, Mohini of slender waist, O king,
Dharmangada replied, having seen and bowed, standing before her: "Take this very thing; do not be doubtful, lady."
Taking a spotless sword and placing it before the king, he said, established in truth and dharma:

Father, there should be no delay in my falling. Make true my mother's word, O king, and the promise.
naradapuran:157:59	One should guard oneself by means of wealth and wives or even one's own sons; a child is for dharma, desire and wealth of a king who desires welfare.
naradapuran:157:60	My death for your sake gives an imperishable goal; and your worlds will be pleasant by keeping your own word.
naradapuran:157:61	Giving up the great sorrow arising from killing a son, my beginning of giving up the body will happen in a man's body,
naradapuran:157:62	free of all disease, equal to Indra, O lord. Those who are killed for their father, for their mother,
naradapuran:157:63	for cow or Brahmin or woman, O king, for land or kings or gods,
naradapuran:157:64	for a child or a disabled one, go to shining worlds. Enough of this distress; strike me with the best sword.
naradapuran:157:65	Keep the truth, O king, and do not eat on Hari's day. One should kill a son or even a wife for dharma, O king.
naradapuran:157:66	It is heard in the Vedic sayings that, in a sacrifice, one may kill a son; in the best sacrifice, the horse-sacrifice, no fault arises, O king.
naradapuran:157:67	Whatever Mohini, my mother, says, you must surely do without hesitation.
naradapuran:157:68	Be gracious, O king; do the word I speak, truly for my own death; free yourself, O king, from the very dreadful untruth of speech, through contact with Mohini's hand.
naradapuran:157:69	By your killing your son, O lord of the earth, your fame will be made manifest, and from the manifestation of fame, O father, there will be fame that is imperishable, without doubt.
Hearing Mohini's words, "Eat, do not kill your offspring; do not eat; kill your son," (the king) held fast in insistence.
At that very time the Lord, lotus-eyed, hidden, stayed in the sky, watching the firmness,
of the three, O tiger among kings: cloud-dark, stainless, of the hero Dharmangada and of Rukmangada,
together with Sandhyavali. Janardana, in the sky, when Mohini had said "eat, eat",
the king took the spotless sword to kill his son Dharmangada. Dharmangada, ornament of dharma, with a very glad mind, bowed to the Garuda-bannered Lord, and seeing his father with sword in hand,
bowing to mother and father and to the discus-bearing God, the best of kings, looking at his mother's piteous face,
Dharmangada then placed his neck on the ground, a conch-like neck, even, golden, very soft,
with many lines, thick, and showed it in the path of the sword, out of devotion to his father and still more to his mother.
As the king was giving up his son's neck, filled with the joy of the moon-faced Mohini, with the sword in hand, the Lord of the world, the whole earth with mountains trembled.
The ocean swelled at once, to drown the three worlds. Hundreds of meteors fell on earth with thunderclaps and lightning from the sky.
Mohini became pale: "I have not done the gods' work. My birth is now fruitless, made so by Fate, maker of the world.
This bewildering form of mine is a mockery, for the king has not eaten on Hari's day, which removes fear of sin; I shall be equal to straws in heaven.
He of great strength will go the path of liberation; I, sinful, shall go to dreadful hell."
As the king raised the sword, O tiger among kings, Mohini, overcome by delusion, fell on the ground.
The king too, shining with that sword, was ready to cut the neck of Vrishangada's... Dharmangada, his son.
The king, steady and gold-ornamented, with great joy cut off his son's face with its earrings, lovely, moon-bright, shining —
just then, the king was seized by the hand by the Lord, husband of the daughter of the Milk Ocean: "I am pleased, I am pleased, without doubt; go to my world, Lord of the world,
with your beloved, with your son, having established your fame on earth, pure and white, worshipped by the three worlds, setting your foot on Yama's head, O king.
Go to my abode, called body (of Vishnu)." The king, touched by the discus-bearer's hand, became stainless, with his beloved and his son.
He came swiftly and went to the divine body of the God, that great king, leaving the earth-born Lakshmi, leaving maidservants, fine wealth and treasury,
leaving elephants, horses and chariots, his own wives and kinsmen, and went to the body of Madhusudana; then a shower of flowers fell from the sky.
Delighted Siddhas and guardians of the world struck drums which resounded; they sang lovely songs, O king, and celestial women danced joyfully.
Gandharva maidens, pleased by the king's deed, and the sun's son, seeing that wonder, saw the king, with wife and son, enter Hari's body, having wiped away his writing,
and having made all the worlds go the way pointed by the king, to grateful Hari-world paths, he again, afraid, approached Pitamaha and said weeping to the four-faced God:
Lord, I shall not be an official; I am without command, Lord of the world of gods. Appoint another, I do something else, father; let there be no punishment on me.

For a year, large-eyed one, worshipped with the Krichchhra practice — his attainment is incomparable, that he did not move from truth.
naradapuran:159:30	The woman who obstructs the king is praised in the worlds, but one who sets her mind in deed, mind and speech on killing her son,
naradapuran:159:31	raised a sword and abandoned affection, very far — the Lord Madhusudana, having tested such a test,
naradapuran:159:32	the king who would kill his dear son and does not eat on Hari's day, seeing the feeling of the son, the beloved and the king,
naradapuran:159:33	Vishnu, pleased in the afterworld, led the three to his abode, with their bodies, their karma exhausted, like a fire-brand lit.
naradapuran:159:34	If the fruit of an undertaking is not accomplished, goddess, though effort was made, what fault is yours here now?
naradapuran:159:35	For this reason all the boon-giving gods have arrived, auspicious one; in success or failure, a doer of action is not in vain.
naradapuran:159:36	A servant is to be maintained by a king wishing dharma; if a deed is not accomplished though one strove with good will,
naradapuran:159:37	only wages are to be given, and satisfaction would not be the fruit. He who does not give his livelihood to him for his living
naradapuran:159:38	gets the sin of cow-killing, without doubt. Therefore, fair-hipped one, give what is desired, beautiful one.
naradapuran:159:39	The gods, having acted with sincere intent, will make an obstacle; what do the gods not do with you, fair-faced one?
naradapuran:159:40	By the power of Dvadashi, the destroyer of obstacles was broken. Thus addressed by the gods, Mohini, bewilderer of the world,
cheerless, bereft of her husband, very unhappy, said: "Cursed is this life of mine, by which the task has not been accomplished.
The crowding of people on Yama's road, O lords of the immortals, was not made; Hari's day was not erased; no one ate on Hari's day.
By that hero king, a son was killed gladly; Rukmangada, having put his foot on my head, went to Hari.
Vishnu, of immeasurable qualities, stainless, the support of the stainless, the Swan, the pure state, sky, Om, the imperishable seed,
formless, without appearance, free of the world-spread, stainless, void, of the nature of space, devoid of meditator and meditation,
of whom they say 'He is' or 'He is not', who is neither far nor near, the supreme abode, grasped by the mind, called Purusha, made of the world,
seated in the heart-lotus, eternal, of the nature of light — when that one is attained, what is the fruit of my life?
The man who takes wages when the work is not accomplished, abandoning his master, surely goes to hell.
Servants of gods who do not accomplish the masters' work, eating wages, are born as horses on earth.
This work of mine, unaccomplished, destroyer of husband and son — how shall I take a boon from you, dwellers in heaven?"
The gods said: "Say, Mohini, we shall give what is wished in your heart. We shall be freed of debt, having done you a favour.
You made effort, goddess, for the king's purpose; you share the fruit of the one who acted for such a purpose."
While the gods were thus speaking, O king, the royal priest, bright as fire, came from the king (of the gods).
The sage had been living in the middle of water, devoted to pranayama; when twelve years were complete, he came out of the water.
Having come out, he heard of Mohini's doings, O king; the tiger among sages, angry, approached the host of gods.
He said to all the gods who were giving a boon to Mohini: "Shame on this one! Shame on the host of gods! Shame on the deed called sin!
It causes the destruction of your states; it makes grow the aims of men, and you are the givers of the boon Mohini desired,
she who is joined with killing, who destroys husband and son, who is without livelihood, a heap of ... — for her there is no purification in this world, O gods, even by falling into a kindled fire."

Killing a husband is fruitless; this, equal to the best Brahmins' ... done before; for her there is no purification here even by falling into a fire kindled with fuel, O gods. Freeing Rukmangada, the ornament of dharma, by nectar-words, with his beloved to the state of liberation, having killed her, he made the earth without a king.

Nor is there a dwelling in hell, gods, nor a place for this dull-minded one in heaven; nor do the gods approach near the king, nor does she reach the imperishable abode of Vishnu.
naradapuran:159:61	Nor, defiled by worldly gossip, can she dwell anywhere in the worlds. Shame on the life, O gods, of one reproached in deeds and ever engaged in sin.
naradapuran:159:62	Having killed her husband, son, and a co-wife who was like a mother, or having killed the whole earth, to what end, gods, will she go?
naradapuran:159:63	This one is more sinful, O gods, a destroyer of Hari's dharma; she always said, 'Eat on Hari's day,'
naradapuran:159:64	for the nourishment of life, and even they go to a low state: 'Eat on Vishnu's day, kill a cow with a Brahmin.'
naradapuran:159:65	Having drunk what is not to be drunk, how can one get a dwelling in heaven? This is told for the ignorant; for the knowing there is no decision.
naradapuran:159:66	For a word uttered in ignorance — 'Eat on Hari's day' — purification is declared even for that by a hundred pranayamas,
naradapuran:159:67	or by fasting on Ekadashi, O gods, or by a bath in the Jyeshtha-kunda with the star, joined,
naradapuran:159:68	or touching the Shukara, or worship of the gods; it is told by the Brahmins; this one is exceedingly cruel today.
naradapuran:159:69	Devoted to sin in eating on Vishnu's day, hard to approach, setting aside her husband's word and having her dear son killed,
naradapuran:159:70	the son who knew words, devoted to words, devoted to the welfare of mothers — she is the destroyer of Vishnu's dharma, full of much sin.
naradapuran:159:71	She is not to be touched, O lords of gods; how can you be givers of boons to her? You are devoted to the just and the righteous.
naradapuran:159:72	The gods do not protect one joined with sin; gods are held the support of dharma, and dharma is established in the Veda.
naradapuran:159:73	By the Vedas, service to the husband is declared the dharma of women. Whatever the husband says, that should be done without hesitation.
naradapuran:159:74	They should say 'white' of white, and 'black' of black, immortals; that is to be known as service; mere attendance is not service.
naradapuran:159:75	The husband's command was broken, O gods, wishing to establish her own command; therefore Mohini is sinful of all women, without doubt. The king, bound by oaths for accomplishing truth,
naradapuran:159:76	said various words; the killer of her son did not wish it. By that the king went to liberation, leaving sin in her.
naradapuran:159:77	This one is sin-bodied, joined with killing.

The giver of all gifts, devoted to Brahmins, whose god is Hari, who loves to please his subjects, who serves Hari's day,
naradapuran:159:79	unattached to other men's wives, without desire for objects, who gives up desire for others' sake, who always serves sacrifices,
naradapuran:159:80	always on earth engaged in subduing the wicked, a king not seized by the seven dreadful vices —
naradapuran:159:81	having thrown him away, how will this ill-conducted one be fit for a boon? Whoever, god or demon, stays on her side,
naradapuran:159:82	I would reduce him to ashes in a moment, O best of gods. And whoever among the gods makes an effort to protect Mohini,
naradapuran:159:83	the sin that is lodged in Mohini arises in him.
Having said this, the best of Brahmins, taking fierce water in his hand, looked in anger at the Creator's daughter and cast it on her head, blazing like fire.
As soon as the water was cast, O king, her body blazed at once, as the gods looked on, like a grass-blade licked by flames of fire.
Withdraw your wrath, withdraw it, Lord! — as the voices of the Maruts in the sky said this, that fire, wiped by the Brahmin's word, left the woman only ashes.

Father, I have no place in the three worlds with their moving and unmoving; wherever I go, they drive me away.
naradapuran:160:22	I was banished by the people, struck firmly with weapons; taking your command I went to the gold-adorned Rukmangada.
naradapuran:160:23	This deed resolved by me is censured by all the worlds: having troubled my husband and killed my son with the best sword,
naradapuran:160:24	having agitated Sandhyavali, father, this plight has come to me. There is no goal now for me, a sinner, O God.
naradapuran:160:25	Especially I am a sharer of sorrow, born through a Brahmin's curse. For those struck by a Brahmin's word, for those burned by fire,
naradapuran:160:26	for those killed by Divakirti (outcastes), for those eaten by animals and the like, for those who died in the Shatahrada — the golden river is the giver of liberation, father.
naradapuran:160:27	If you, with the gods, propitiate that Brahmin who gave the curse out of love for me, then a goal is prepared for me.
To her speaking so, O king, Brahma, grandfather of the world, with Shiva, Indra, Dharma, Surya, Agni and the lords of gods and sages,
placing Mohini in front, went to the Brahmin. Arriving there, O protector of the earth, Brahma surrounded by gods and others,
with great honour himself bowed. O king, Pitamaha is to be worshipped and honoured by Rudra and the other gods;
deluded, for Mohini's sake he himself made salutation. When a great task has arisen, impossible in the three worlds,
the greeting of a younger person is not blamed, O king. That Brahmin, master of the Vedas and Vedangas, established in austerity,
seeing the maker of the worlds come with the gods, rose and bowed to Brahma, the sages and the gods,
seated them with devotion and praised the lotus-born. Then the Lord, maker of the world, teacher of the world, pleased,
the gods begged that Brahmin, honoured by the king, for Mohini: "Dear Brahmin, of good conduct, benefactor of the other world,
show mercy, ocean of mercy; be the giver of a goal to Mohini. She was sent by me, O Brahmin, to bewilder Rukmangada.
My daughter, seeing Yama's world empty, O honourer, and Vaikuntha crowded with all the untroubled people,
was produced by mind, the goddess doing good to the gods. Hear, O god on earth, what I tell you:
the very subtle course of dharma that does good to the world. By this fair-limbed one, having tested the gold-adorned,
with wife and son, Brahmin, he was brought to Hari's abode — the king struck by devotion by observing Hari's day.
Yama's place was made empty by the work of wiping the ledger. A harm done to the gods, O Brahmin sage, cannot be endured by those born from arms;
especially those who went with him as his companions, among the Brahmins.
What cannot be reached by the Sankhya-knower nor by eightfold yoga but by devotion, that was got by the Brahmin-king's husband, his son and his co-wife.
What was opposed to the conduct of that meritorious king, crest-jewel of kings, by the force of that sin she fled, left as ashes, burned by your curse.
She acted for the gods, for increase of the world, and for the king's benefit; not seeking her own aim, she gets an insult. How, O twice-born, forgive her wrong.

Show mercy and take peace; grinding what is ground is not in keeping with policy. She has been struck down by your curse; show favour; be the giver of her goal, you, in whose act this Mohini would give up her cruel intention toward you the sacrificer."
